newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Kia creditors pledge loans, but conditions remain.
newsitem.headline: Kia creditors pledge loans, but conditions remain.

text.p: Creditor banks to South Korea's Kia Group on Monday agreed to grant emergency loans to core units of the troubled conglomerate but only under conditions the group has repeatedly rejected.

Ryoo Shee-yul, president of main creditor Korea First Bank, said creditor banks agreed to grant 183.1 billion won ($205.9 million) in emergency loans to four of the group's affiliates, including flagship Kia Motors Corp.

But those loans would be granted only when the group's top executives tendered resignation letters and the labour union agreed in writing to freeze their wages and reduce the number of employees, Ryoo told reporters.
The union has agreed but insisted it would withdraw from the agreement if creditors forced executives to resign or allowed a third party to take over Kia.
"The conditions should be met for the group to get emergency funds," said Ryoo. "There is talk that banks want to replace the management immediately, but it's a misunderstanding."
He said banks just wanted to confirm that the management was determined to overcome the crisis, which surfaced on July 15 when creditors decided to protect Kia Group from an immediate failure.
Both Kia Group chairman Kim Sun-hong and the labour union have refused the resignation demand, saying creditors really wanted to sell off the group to a third party.
Analysts said Monday's developments showed the Kia Group was in a stronger position than creditors.

"Unless banks give up their position, we could see a domino effect among subcontractors. In that sense, the situation is favouring Kia now," said Kang Hun-sok, auto analyst at ING Baring Securities. "There's too much at stake to let Kia go."

Creditors also agreed the bailout protection period for the nation's eighth-largest conglomerate would continue until September 29 without condition. During the period, the group would be exempted from servicing debts.
Kia's troubles are of special concern because of the group's huge debts and the potential for a ripple effect at a time when the country is in an economic slump that has yet to bottom out.
Kia owed some 9.54 trillion won to financial institutions as at the end of May, compared to the Jinro Group's 3.2 trillion won and the Dainong Group's 1.84 trillion won.
Jinro and Dainong are the only two other groups to be put under protection by their creditor banks.
Ryoo also said creditors had seriously taken into account the overall economic impact of the group's troubles.
"There was a strong call among banks to drop protection for the group, but we have taken into account the economic situation and agreed to uphold our earlier decision," said Ryoo.
Kia Motors, freed from the constraints of the group's weaker units, might be able to stand on its own, analyst Kang said.
"I think Kia Motors will survive at least in the short-term. The question is whether it can succeed in the medium- or long-term," he said.
The Kia Group, with 38 affiliates both at home and abroad, recorded a combined net loss of 129.4 billion won in calendar 1996 on combined sales of 12.1 trillion won.
